disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder with psychotic features is characterized by at least one full manic episode, often alternating with major depressive episodes, in which mood disturbance is severe enough to cause marked impairment or require hospitalization. During the most intense phases of mania or depression, individuals may experience delusions or hallucinations that are typically mood-congruent (e.g., grandiose themes in mania, guilt or worthlessness in depression), though they can also be mood-incongruent. The course is usually recurrent and episodic, with symptom-free intervals varying widely between individuals, and onset often in late adolescence or early adulthood but possible later in life. It is distinguished from schizoaffective or primary psychotic disorders by the temporal relationship of psychosis to clear mood episodes and from unipolar depression by the presence of at least one manic episode.

narrative.stressor: Over the past year, Milagros gradually took on more caregiving responsibilities for her husband after his diabetes worsened and he developed mobility issues, leaving her coordinating medical appointments on top of her extensive volunteer work and family commitments. In preparation for a major Día de los Muertos festival she was co-chairing, she began pushing herself to stay up later with her nightly tea, obsessively reworking event details and cutting back on rest, while also worrying about her own blood pressure and memory after a recent borderline lab result. Family members noticed a pronounced shift when her usual meticulous planning escalated into increasingly grand, inflexible ideas about expanding the festival and her role as a "guardian" of Oaxacan culture, along with growing mistrust of others’ input and strain in her church relationships. After two months of escalating interpersonal conflict at the community center, arguments at home over money she redirected into festival expenses, and neighbors expressing concern about her suspicious comments about being monitored, her adult daughter accompanied her to an urgent psychiatric evaluation at the insistence of their parish priest and primary care physician.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My family keeps saying my beliefs about the festival and people watching me aren’t real, but I know they’re true and I can’t be convinced otherwise.”

narrative.stressor: Juan’s symptoms emerged in the context of finishing high school while starting his first job as a healthcare support worker, juggling night shifts, exam pressure for upcoming CNA certification, and expectations from his parents to help with household expenses. Initially energized by the responsibility and overtime pay, he began volunteering for extra shifts, cutting back on sleep, and spending more time sketching ambitious career plans, while his friends noticed a sharp change from his usual calm methodical demeanor to impatient intensity about work and future success. Over several weeks, his ideas about his role in the hospital and his ability to 'revolutionize' patient care grew increasingly unrealistic, leading to conflicts with senior staff when he disregarded instructions and an incident where he stayed late charting unnecessary details without authorization. After a period of this heightened state culminated in him being written up at work and then crashing into a withdrawn, low-functioning phase where he struggled to get out of bed and missed multiple shifts, his supervisor and school counselor jointly urged his parents to seek a psychiatric evaluation when he admitted he no longer trusted his judgment and felt he was "either way too wired or completely wiped out."
narrative.chief_complaint: “For weeks I’ve had this nonstop drive to take on more at the hospital, like I can’t slow my mind or body down even when I know it’s too much.”

narrative.stressor: Lorraine’s difficulties intensified during the year she decided to expand her freelance choreography into a full-time studio, signing a lease for a small space in Bozeman and taking on loans she found both exciting and vaguely overwhelming. What began as her characteristic last-minute planning became a sustained period of increasingly extreme schedules—late-night rehearsals, spontaneous road trips to scout outdoor sites, and impulsive commitments to multiple festivals—leaving her studio finances and class structure in disarray. Friends and collaborators grew alarmed when she started speaking about receiving special messages from the mountains guiding her work and making studio decisions based on these experiences, while she stopped responding to emails from venues and missed grant deadlines, jeopardizing her reputation. After two months in which her business partner threatened to dissolve their agreement, students dropped out over erratic class times, and she then swung into a demoralized spell where she cancelled workshops and stayed home, a close friend finally convinced her to see a psychiatrist by framing it as getting support to save her studio and make sense of the unsettling experiences she was having on her hikes.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Out on the trails and even back in town, I keep hearing and sensing things from the landscape telling me what to do with my work, and it’s starting to scare me.”
